extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity advocates, journal editors, and informed members of the academic community
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and expectations for how scholarly journals should detect, investigate, correct, and communicate about research misconduct (retractions, corrections, expressions of concern, handling of image/data fabrication). Focuses on editorial duties and transparency in academic publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retract fraudulent papers when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should retract papers that are demonstrably fraudulent or when authors’ institutions request retraction (i.e., correct the scientific record by removing invalid work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites Science's 2016 refusal to follow a university’s request to retract a fraudulent paper by Olivier Voinnet as an example of poor practice. Guidance implied: do not refuse legitimate retraction requests; when evidence and institutional findings support retraction, publish a full retraction rather than leaving the paper in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue Editorial Expression of Concern (EEoC) promptly when retraction is delayed
rubrics_metrics.description: When retraction cannot immediately occur (e.g., not all authors agree or institutional investigations are ongoing), journals should publish an Editorial Expression of Concern to alert readers quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Holden Thorp: an EEoC can 'quickly alert readers that concerns have been raised about the reported work' to 'help mitigate the waste of time, effort, and funds.' The article criticizes Science for failing to issue EEoCs in many cases flagged publicly (Elisabeth Bik examples), so journals should use EEoCs consistently and promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish formal corrections transparently (not hidden in supplements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections must be clearly visible, formally published, and linked to the original article rather than buried in supplemental material without independent identifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author documents that Science has 'discreetly hid corrections inside the supplemental material, without attributing a DOI,' which makes papers appear 'pristine' to casual readers. Best practice: publish corrections with DOIs and make them discoverable and clearly associated with the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact authors' institutions and actively verify original/raw data
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should reach out to the authors' home institutions and request/raw_data as part of misconduct investigations, rather than relying solely on public allegations or authors' statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Elisabeth Bik flagged problems in Sijen et al. 2007 and evidence that Science did not contact the Hubrecht Institute; later the institute conducted an investigation and retrieved archives. Guidance: journals must contact institutions promptly and request original data to verify concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond promptly and constructively to whistleblowers and image sleuths
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial offices should take reports from external watchdogs (e.g., PubPeer, image analysts like Elisabeth Bik) seriously and investigate them rather than ignoring or dismissing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page details multiple cases where Bik posted evidence and 'the journal just didn’t care.' Good practice: have a clear process to receive, triage, and act on external reports; editors should be accessible and responsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat all authors equally regardless of stature or institutional prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions about corrections/retractions should not be swayed by the prominence of the authors (Nobel laureates, university presidents, influential scientists) or by institutional clout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives many examples (Gallo, Baltimore, Tessier-Lavigne, Plasterk) where high-profile authors apparently avoided correction. Guidance: avoid preferential treatment; apply misconduct policies uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not outsource final responsibility for retraction to authors/universities
rubrics_metrics.description: While institutional findings are important, journals should not abdicate their editorial responsibility and must act proactively when evidence indicates serious problems, even if not all authors agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holden Thorp's statement that 'Science journals prefer to publish a retraction signed by all authors' is contrasted with criticism that this approach leaves the literature uncorrected. Guidance: journals should pursue investigations and, when warranted, retract unilaterally rather than waiting indefinitely for unanimous author consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure corrections and retractions are discoverable and properly documented (DOI, links, clear notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections, errata, EEoCs, and retractions should be clearly indexed, carry stable identifiers, and be easy for readers and indexers to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes 'secret corrections' hidden in supplements without DOIs. Best practice: assign DOIs, update article metadata, and link notices prominently on the original article page so databases and readers are alerted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid issuing dishonest or insufficient errata—correct substantive image/data problems fully
rubrics_metrics.description: Errata must fully and honestly address the specific problems (e.g., image duplication, splicing, Photoshop) rather than offering minimal or misleading text that fails to correct the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Dalkara (2013) paper had an erratum the author calls 'a very dishonest Erratum.' Guidance: when figures are manipulated (duplicated bands, splicing), provide corrected figures, detailed explanations, and if conclusions are affected consider stronger measures (correction with clear details, EEoC, or retraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accessible editorial contact information and transparency about handling concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should make themselves contactable (email/address) and be transparent about how concerns are handled, timelines, and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorp publicly provided his email and said 'I immediately responded with mine.' The author views accessibility positively. Guidance: publish clear contact points and processes for reporting integrity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on evidence posted on public platforms (PubPeer, Twitter) rather than ignoring it
rubrics_metrics.description: Public allegations and forensic analyses posted on platforms like PubPeer or social media should trigger editorial review and not be dismissed solely because they originate outside formal channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author documents many PubPeer posts and tweets (Elisabeth Bik) that apparently prompted no response from Science. Journals should monitor these platforms and document their responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate and correct image manipulation and data fabrication specifically (e.g., cloned gel bands, Photoshop hacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must have procedures and expertise (or access to forensic experts) to evaluate allegations of image manipulation and fabricated data and apply appropriate remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article catalogs repeated instances of cloned gel bands, flipped/cloned images, and Photoshop 'hack jobs' across multiple papers. Guidance: use image-forensics, request original blots/raw images, and publish substantive corrections or retractions when manipulation is confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and require availability of original/raw data archives
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and journals should preserve original data and be able to produce it upon request; lack of raw data can justify retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update note: Sijen et al. 2007 was retracted 'due to absence of raw data.' Guidance: journals should require retention and accessibility of raw data and act when archives are missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize integrity of the scholarly record over reputational or institutional relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions should prioritize correcting the literature and protecting readers over preserving relationships with elite authors, societies, or institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues Science sometimes 'pretends there is nothing wrong' to avoid displeasing 'AAAS grandees' and documents continued celebration of figures like Gallo despite serious past issues. Guidance: avoid conflicts of interest and prioritize the public record.
